name: Vils
kurzbeschreibung: Tiniest town in Tirol with a medieval old town, the Vilsbrücke, and a historic tannery past.
beschreibung:
Overview

Vils is situated at an elevation of 826 meters in the Tyrolean Außerfern right on the Bavarian border with the Allgäu, hugging the Vils River just before its confluence with the Lech. Enclosed between the rugged limestone crags of the Tannheim Mountains—crowned by the Vilser Kegel at 1,831 meters—and the Allgäu Alps, Vils counts among the smallest chartered towns in Austria with roughly 1,500 residents. This historic town seamlessly blends more than seven centuries of municipal heritage, medieval street alignments, Hohenstaufen castle romance, a proud limestone quarrying legacy, and immediate proximity to Bavaria's fairy-tale royal castles of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau.

History

Vils was first documented in 1327 as 'Fülß'. In that same year, King Louis the Bavarian granted Peter of Hohenegg city rights for Vils, patterned after the imperial free city of Kaufbeuren. The noble Lords of Hohenegg governed from nearby Castle Vilsegg under enfeoffment from Kempten Abbey. In 1408, Duke Frederick IV of Austria secured feudal supremacy, though Vils only became permanently integrated into Tyrol in 1816 following the Napoleonic upheavals. Overlooking the valley on a wooded limestone crag stand the ruins of Castle Vilsegg: erected around 1220–1230, this Hohenstaufen stronghold featuring an imposing keep built with finely dressed rusticated ashlar stones ranks among the finest examples of medieval fortress design in Tyrol. In the town center, the Parish Church of the Assumption showcases splendid Baroque architecture begun in 1709, attributed to master Johann Jakob Herkommer. In 1899, the Schretter family founded Schretter & Cie, creating Tyrol's sole cement works and sparking lasting industrial vitality.

Getting There

By car, Vils is reached toll-free from Germany via motorway A7 through the Füssen border tunnel and the B179/B314 in just a few minutes. From Tyrol, the B179 leads over the Fern Pass and through Reutte directly into Vils. Train passengers benefit from two stations on the scenic Außerfernbahn railway line: Bahnhof Vils and the centrally located Vils Stadt stop provide direct connections to Kempten in the Allgäu, Reutte, Garmisch-Partenkirchen, and Munich.

Tips

A family-friendly historic walk ascends from the old town to the ruins of Castle Vilsegg, offering sweeping vistas across the Vils Valley; at the base of the hill, Saint Anne's chapel and an ancient hammer forge merit a visit. Culture seekers should explore the Museum of the Town of Vils, highlighting local violin-making traditions and town history. A popular alpine hike climbs through the forest to the rustic Vilser Alm refuge at 1,226 meters, serving homemade Tyrolean dumplings. Upstream, visitors can witness the plunging waters of the Vilsfall waterfall, while Füssen, Lake Alatsee, and Neuschwanstein Castle are quickly reached by bicycle.
